landmarks.name: Great Wall of China
landmarks.writeup: An ancient series of walls and fortifications stretching over 13,000 miles, built to protect Chinese states from invasions.

wiki.extract: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications in China. They were built across the historical northern borders of ancient Chinese states and Imperial China as protection against various nomadic groups from the Eurasian Steppe. The first walls date to the 7th century BC; these were joined together in the Qin dynasty. Successive dynasties expanded the wall system; the best-known sections were built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644).

landmarks.name: Forbidden City
landmarks.writeup: A vast imperial palace complex in Beijing that served as the home of emperors and political center for centuries.

wiki.extract: The Forbidden City is the imperial palace complex in the center of the Imperial City in Beijing, China. It was the residence of 24 Ming and Qing dynasty Emperors, and the center of political power in China for over 500 years from 1420 to 1924. The palace is now administered by the Palace Museum and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. The Forbidden City is one of the most famous palaces in all of Chinese history, and is the largest preserved royal palace complex still standing in the world.

landmarks.name: Terracotta Army
landmarks.writeup: Thousands of life-sized clay soldiers buried with China's first Emperor Qin Shi Huang to protect him in the afterlife.

wiki.extract: The Terracotta Army is a collection of terracotta sculptures depicting the armies of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China. It is a form of funerary art buried with the emperor in 210–209 BCE in his mausoleum with the purpose of protecting him in his afterlife.

landmarks.name: Potala Palace
landmarks.writeup: A historic palace in Lhasa, Tibet, that was the winter residence of the Dalai Lama and a symbol of Tibetan Buddhism.

wiki.extract: Potala Palace is a museum complex in Lhasa, the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. It was formerly the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas, built in the dzong style on Marpo Ri. From 1649 until 1959 it served as the Dalai Lamas' residence, after which it became chiefly a museum following the annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China.

landmarks.name: Shanghai Tower
landmarks.writeup: The tallest building in China and the second tallest in the world, symbolizing China's rapid modernization.

wiki.extract: The Shanghai Tower is a 128-story, 632-meter-tall (2,073-foot) megatall skyscraper located in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. It is currently the tallest building in China, and the world's third-tallest building by height to architectural top. It was the tallest and largest LEED-CS Platinum certified building in the world from 2016 to 2025. It was also the second tallest-building in the world, from 2015 to 2021, until the completion of Merdeka 118 in Malaysia. The Shanghai Tower also had the world's fastest elevators at a top speed of 20.5 meters per second until 2017, when it was surpassed by the Guangzhou CTF Finance Center, with its top speed of 21 meters per second.

cultural_events.name: Chinese New Year
cultural_events.writeup: Also known as Spring Festival, it marks the lunar new year with family reunions, fireworks, and traditional performances.

wiki.extract: Chinese New Year, also known as the Spring Festival, marks the beginning of a new year on the traditional lunisolar Chinese calendar. It is one of the most important holidays in Chinese culture. Marking the end of winter and the beginning of spring, this festival takes place from Chinese New Year's Eve to the Lantern Festival, held on the 15th day of the year. The first day of the Chinese New Year falls on the new moon that appears between 21 January and 20 February.

cultural_events.name: Mid-Autumn Festival
cultural_events.writeup: Celebrated with mooncakes and lanterns, it honors the harvest and the full moon.

wiki.extract: The Mid-Autumn Festival, also known as the Moon Festival or Mooncake Festival, is a harvest festival celebrated in Chinese culture. It occurs on the 15th day of the 8th month of the Chinese lunisolar calendar and can fall between 7 September and 8 October (inclusive) of the Gregorian calendar. On this day, the Chinese believe that the moon is at its fullest and brightest, coinciding with the time of harvest in the middle of autumn.

cultural_events.name: Dragon Boat Festival
cultural_events.writeup: Commemorates the poet Qu Yuan with boat races and eating zongzi (sticky rice dumplings).

wiki.extract: The Dragon Boat Festival, also known as the Duanwu Festival or Tuen Ng Festival, is a traditional Chinese holiday that occurs on the fifth day of the fifth month of the Chinese calendar, which corresponds to late May or early June in the Gregorian calendar. The holiday commemorates Qu Yuan who was the beloved prime minister of the southern Chinese state of Chu during the Warring States period, about 600 B.C. to 200 B.C., and is celebrated by holding dragon boat races and eating sticky rice dumplings called zongzi, which were southern Chinese traditions. The Dragon Boat Festival integrates praying for good luck and taking respite from the summer heat.

food_writeup: Chinese cuisine is diverse, featuring regional styles such as Sichuan's spicy dishes, Cantonese dim sum, and northern wheat-based foods. Staple ingredients include rice, noodles, soy products, and a variety of meats and vegetables.
brief_history: China is one of the world's oldest civilizations, with recorded history dating back over 3,000 years. It has experienced dynastic rule, imperial expansion, colonial encounters, a communist revolution in 1949, and rapid economic growth in recent decades.

commentary.inflation_management: China's inflation has been low and well-contained by global standards, managed through a mix of administered prices, a managed exchange rate, capital controls, and People's Bank of China liquidity operations. It peaked at 5.87% in 2008 on the commodity boom, then stayed in the 1-3% range through the 2010s, with a pork-driven bump to 5.4% in 2011 and 2.89% in 2019. Since 2023 the problem has inverted: inflation fell to 0.23% in 2023, 0.21% in 2024, and a projected 0.01% in 2025 as property-sector distress, weak consumption, and overcapacity produced deflationary pressure. The PBoC has eased repeatedly but transmission is blunted by debt overhangs and cautious banks.
commentary.debt_management: The debt story is the central macro concern: general government gross debt rose from 25.2% of GDP in 2006 to a projected 96.3% in 2025, with the steepest climbs after the 2008 stimulus (33.98% by 2009), the 2015-16 re-leveraging (49.7% in 2016), and COVID (69.0% in 2020 to 82.0% in 2023). The official ratio understates the burden because local-government financing vehicles carry large off-balance-sheet liabilities. GDP still grew enormously, from $2.8tn to a projected $19.4tn, which has kept ratios serviceable, but the marginal productivity of debt-financed investment has fallen sharply.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis; a 4-trillion-yuan stimulus powered recovery but seeded the debt boom.
Stock-market crash and surprise yuan devaluation rattled global markets; capital controls tightened.
US-China trade war imposed tariffs and accelerated supply-chain diversification talk.
COVID-19: strict lockdowns, then a fast rebound that made China the only major growing economy that year.
Property-sector crackdown; Evergrande's default marked the start of a prolonged real-estate crisis.
Zero-COVID lockdowns (notably Shanghai) hit growth; policy abruptly reversed in December.
Deflationary pressure and property distress persisted despite repeated stimulus measures.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: China faces a structural slowdown: aging demographics, property-sector deleveraging, and local-government debt constrain growth toward 3-4%, with deflation risk lingering if consumption stays weak. Offsets include manufacturing upgrading, green tech, and AI investment. Geopolitical decoupling and tariffs are a persistent drag. The analytical risk is a Japan-style balance-sheet stagnation if debt is not restructured decisively; the upside is successful rebalancing toward consumption, which policy has so far struggled to deliver.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
